heading: Delta trade to national awakening
body: Bengal's history turns on geography twice over: first as a delta where the Ganges and Brahmaputra meet the sea, which made it one of the subcontinent's richest trading regions for over a thousand years and drew Mughal governors, European trading companies and pirates alike; and second as the place where British colonial power in India was headquartered and, eventually, first seriously challenged. Calcutta (now Kolkata) began as a cluster of villages the East India Company fortified in the late 17th century, and grew through the 18th and 19th centuries into the empire's second city after London — the commercial and administrative capital of British India.

That concentration of colonial institutions, printing presses and English-language education produced the Bengal Renaissance of the 19th century: a wave of social and intellectual reform led by figures such as Raja Ram Mohan Roy, who campaigned against sati, and later Ishwar Chandra Vidyasagar and Rabindranath Tagore, whose writing helped define modern Bengali literature and who became Asia's first Nobel laureate in 1913. The same period produced a modern Bengali press, new schools of Bengali painting and theatre, and a wave of political organizing that made Bengal central to the early Indian independence movement.

That political weight is also why the British moved the imperial capital away from it. The 1905 partition of Bengal along religious lines provoked mass protest and boycotts of British goods (the swadeshi movement); the partition was reversed in 1911, and in the same year the British shifted the capital of India from Calcutta to the more centrally located and, they judged, more governable Delhi. Kolkata never fully recovered its former political primacy, but the institutions and built fabric of that century — colonial civic buildings, the reformist and literary societies, Tagore's Santiniketan — remain the throughline for the entries on this map.
